snapshots.name: Montaigne Himself
snapshots.subtitle: The essayist, examining his own mind
snapshots.body: The author's own running self-portrait, the true subject of the Essays. A translator's note preserves the moment he coined the term "popular poetry" in French — a small, telling instance of a mind that constantly names and studies its own operations.

snapshots.name: Death, and Learning to Die
snapshots.subtitle: 'To philosophize is to learn to die'
snapshots.body: The subject of one of Montaigne's most famous essays, which opens by citing Cicero's claim that to study philosophy is nothing but to prepare oneself to die — study being, Montaigne argues, a kind of apprenticeship in separating the soul from the body.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.subtitle: Montaigne's most-cited exemplar
snapshots.body: Montaigne's recurring model of composed, undramatic wisdom — invoked here for his famously offhand answer to Crito, who asked at his death how he wished to be buried, treating the disposal of his body as a matter of supreme indifference.

snapshots.name: Étienne de La Boétie
snapshots.subtitle: Montaigne's late, irreplaceable friend
snapshots.body: The friend whose death Montaigne mourned all his life and whose sayings he quotes throughout the Essays — here credited with calling beauty "a short tyranny," one of the small fragments of La Boétie's mind Montaigne preserves by continuing to converse with him in writing.

snapshots.name: Seneca and Plutarch
snapshots.subtitle: Montaigne's two constant companions
snapshots.body: The Stoic Seneca and the moralist Plutarch, quoted and paraphrased more often than any other authors in the Essays — less as authorities to defer to than as conversation partners Montaigne argues with, borrows from, and measures his own experience against.

snapshots.name: Cato the Younger and Roman Exemplars
snapshots.subtitle: Ancient models of constancy
snapshots.body: Cato the Younger and figures like him — the great men of the Roman civil wars invoked here — serve Montaigne as touchstones for constancy and self-command under extremity, examples he tests as often as he admires.

snapshots.name: "What Do I Know?" (Que Sais-je?)
snapshots.subtitle: Montaigne's chosen motto
snapshots.body: The question Montaigne adopted as his personal motto, borne with the emblem of a pair of scales: a deliberate, working skepticism that treats even the most certain-seeming statement — "it is fine weather" — as a form of speech that can still deceive us.

snapshots.name: The New World and Its Peoples
snapshots.subtitle: 'Of Cannibals'
snapshots.body: The subject of one of the boldest essays: an account, drawn from a servant who had lived years in Brazil, of a people Europeans called barbarous — which Montaigne uses to argue that "barbarism" is mostly a matter of being unlike one's own customs.

snapshots.name: The Power of Custom
snapshots.subtitle: How habit reshapes nature
snapshots.body: The subject of "Of Custom": Montaigne's argument, illustrated by the story of a countrywoman who carried a growing calf every day until she could carry a full-grown ox, that habit can make the most unnatural things feel entirely natural to us.

snapshots.name: The Body and Experience
snapshots.subtitle: Montaigne's late, physical philosophy
snapshots.body: The turn, especially pronounced in the later books, toward the body's own testimony — illness, aging, appetite, and sensation treated as sources of philosophical knowledge in their own right, not distractions from the mind's proper business.
